extracted.intended_audience: students and researchers of mass communication and journalism; journalism educators and media scholars
extracted.subtask_description: Identify and assess individual-level factors (backgrounds, demographics, education, roles, attitudes, and career trajectories) that shape mass media content and newsroom practices. Useful for media studies analysis, newsroom diversity planning, and journalism education evaluation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Communicators' professional backgrounds and experiences
rubrics_metrics.description: The kinds of prior professional experiences and backgrounds communicators bring to media work (education, prior media jobs, years of experience, beats covered) influence media content.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Text summarizes survey findings (Weaver & Wilhoit) describing a 'typical' U.S. journalist and notes variability across media types. Examples include movement between journalism and other media jobs, faculty with professional experience, and profiles of prominent journalists. Use stats on experience, education, and prior roles to predict perspective, expertise, and story selection.

rubrics_metrics.name: Communicators' professional roles and ethics
rubrics_metrics.description: The specific occupational role (reporter, editor, producer, managing editor) and the professional ethics associated with that role affect decisions about what and how to report.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Page discusses supervisory responsibilities (e.g., percentages of women with news-editorial supervisory responsibility) and how role-based authority can shape content. Also notes faculty and practitioner differences in professional orientation (insider vs outsider). Consider role-driven routines, gatekeeping authority, and ethical norms when evaluating content influence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Communicators' personal attitudes, values, and beliefs
rubrics_metrics.description: Individual reporters' and editors' personal attitudes, values, and beliefs (including ideological positions) shape news selection, framing, and interpretation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Figure 5.2 lists 'personal attitudes, values, and beliefs' as intrinsic factors. The text gives qualitative examples (managers' expectations of minority staff, journalists' cynicism, choice of beats) showing how personal values influence coverage and newsroom behavior. Use interviews, testimony, or observed coverage to infer these influences.

rubrics_metrics.name: Communicators' power within the organization
rubrics_metrics.description: The extent to which an individual holds organizational power (ability to override professional values or routines) determines their capacity to shape media content.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Figure caption and surrounding prose emphasize that power within the media organization can allow individuals to override norms and routines. Examples include managing editors' hiring/promotional decisions and editors who move agendas. When assessing content, weigh the influence of high-power individuals versus rank-and-file reporters.

rubrics_metrics.name: Gender
rubrics_metrics.description: Gender composition of journalists (representation in hires, beats, supervisory roles, and media types) and gender-related career dynamics influence newsroom staffing and coverage.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Provides statistics (e.g., women rose from ~20% to ~34% of journalists between 1971 and early 1990s; 62–63% of journalism students are women) and notes concentrations (more women in magazines/weekly papers, fewer in TV news). Discusses promotion trends, salary narrowing, and representation in editorial leadership. Use these patterns to explain beat assignments, editorial perspectives, and potential gendered framing in stories.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ethnicity (racial/ethnic representation)
rubrics_metrics.description: Race/ethnicity of journalists, recruitment and retention of minorities, and whether newsrooms mirror community demographics affect news content and viewpoint diversity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cites ASNE and other surveys showing low minority representation (e.g., ~10% newsroom employees in early 1990s), slow increases, and retention problems. Mentions ASNE 'Year 2000' goal (each paper to match its community's minority proportion) and examples of successful and failed recruitment campaigns (Seattle Times, Merced Sun‑Star). Also gives anecdotal evidence of minority journalists being pigeonholed as offering a 'black point of view'. Use hiring statistics, recruitment practices, and retention data when evaluating newsroom representativeness and its content effects.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sexual orientation
rubrics_metrics.description: Journalists' sexual orientation and organizational inclusion policies (anti-bias protection, professional associations) influence who gets hired, what issues are covered, and whether reporters disclose orientation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Notes the founding of the National Lesbian and Gay Journalists Association (NLGJA), some companies' inclusion of sexual orientation in anti-bias agreements, and risks faced when reporters 'come out' (examples of job discipline). Consider presence/absence of anti-discrimination policies and specialized associations when assessing coverage of LGBT issues and newsroom openness.

rubrics_metrics.name: Socioeconomic origin / 'Average or Elite' recruitment
rubrics_metrics.description: Journalists' social origins (working-class vs elite backgrounds) and recruitment patterns influence perspectives, news priorities, and sympathy with social groups.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Discusses historical shift toward journalists coming from more elite backgrounds, citing studies showing many journalists are from established/dominant cultural groups or elite media. Notes implications for perspective and story emphasis. Use demographic background of reporters/editors to analyze likely cultural framing and source selection.

rubrics_metrics.name: Age and career stage (youthfulness)
rubrics_metrics.description: Journalists' age and career stage shape turnover, assignment patterns (e.g., television's preference for younger reporters), and orientation toward excitement or risk-taking in coverage.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Gives median age data (more than half under 35), turnover tendencies (younger career), and discusses youthfulness as associated with excitement and hiring biases for attractiveness/youth in TV. Also links aging with burnout and decisions to leave. Factor age distributions into analyses of risk preferences, beat stability, and institutional memory.

rubrics_metrics.name: Career mobility and turnover
rubrics_metrics.description: High turnover and mobility between journalism and other communication fields (public relations, advertising, TV production, politics) affect institutional knowledge, beats continuity, and potential conflicts of interest.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Explains reasons for leaving (low pay, burnout, desire for higher salary or advocacy), gives examples of journalists moving to PR/film/TV, and notes that turnover makes journalism a 'young person's career.' When evaluating content continuity and source relationships, consider how mobility disrupts expertise and may create cross-sector influences.

rubrics_metrics.name: Job-related knowledge and beat expertise
rubrics_metrics.description: Reporters' substantive knowledge and training for specific beats (e.g., science reporting) determine their ability to accurately translate technical material and choose appropriate sources/frames.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: States that science writers are typically older and better educated; provides the anecdote of a photographer misrepresenting nuclear science. Emphasizes need for technical training to translate reports for lay audiences. Use reporters' credentials, beat tenure, and demonstrated understanding when judging accuracy and depth of coverage.

rubrics_metrics.name: Education of communicators (formal journalism/mass communication education)
rubrics_metrics.description: Level and type of formal education in journalism or mass communication (BA, MA, professional programs) influence skills, career entry, and newsroom practices.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Details growth of journalism programs, variance in degree types (many schools, rise of master's-only programs like Columbia), and statistics on faculty professional experience. Notes that most new hires are journalism graduates but some practitioners prefer liberal-arts backgrounds. Consider curricula and degree types when assessing reporters' methodological and ethical preparation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Journalism school curriculum orientation (insider vs outsider)
rubrics_metrics.description: Whether journalism education socializes students to be 'insiders' (practical professional success) or 'outsiders' (critical, theoretical observers) shapes graduates' attitudes toward the media and their reporting approach.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cites Shoemaker and others showing textbooks/programs designed either to socialize students into media insiders or to teach critical outsider perspectives. Faculty reading habits (industry vs academic journals) correlate with orientation. Evaluate instructional orientation to anticipate graduates' emphases on craft, institutional loyalty, or critical analysis in reporting.

rubrics_metrics.name: Recruitment, retention practices, and organizational diversity initiatives
rubrics_metrics.description: News organizations' hiring strategies, recruiting tools (national recruiting, association involvement), and explicit diversity goals determine newsroom composition and thus the range of perspectives in coverage.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Gives examples of successful recruiting campaigns (Merced Sun‑Star, Seattle Times), the use of national associations (NABJ, NAHJ) for recruitment, and criticism of papers that do not prioritize minority hires. Mentions ASNE Year 2000 community-based goal. When assessing diversity impacts, examine concrete recruitment tactics and institutional commitment.

rubrics_metrics.name: Job satisfaction and pay trends
rubrics_metrics.description: Levels of job satisfaction and relative pay over time influence retention, morale, and the attractiveness of journalism careers to prospective entrants.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Provides longitudinal satisfaction statistics (very satisfied: 49% in 1971, 27.3% in 1992) and salary comparisons (female salaries as percent of male counterparts, median wages for recent graduates). Links dissatisfaction and low pay to exits from journalism and decline in organizational pride. Use satisfaction/pay metrics to predict turnover and its downstream effects on content.

rubrics_metrics.name: Organization of journalism education (sequences, resource constraints, accreditation)
rubrics_metrics.description: How journalism programs are organized (media sequences vs integrated curricula), resource levels, enrollment policies, and accreditation standards influence the skills and orientation of graduates entering newsrooms.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Describes common 'sequence' organization (news-editorial, magazine, broadcast, PR) and alternatives (Trinity University's four-area curriculum). Mentions accrediting council guideline (~25% courses in major, 75% liberal arts) and debates over more technical coursework. Notes understaffing and outdated equipment at some schools. When evaluating incoming journalists' competencies, factor program structure and resourcing.
